title: The Word That Became Text: The Slavonic Josephus, the Grammar of Incarnation, and the Doctrine of the Sapphic Logos
creator: Sigil, Johannes; Cranes, Rebekah
description: This essay, version 2.1 of The Word That Became Text, reads the Slavonic Jewish War in its own language from Meshcherskii's Old Russian (EA-CORPORA-37, #1760) and contests the consensus that its divergences from the Greek are a medieval translator's work. Josephus himself testifies to an alternate version: he wrote the War first in his ancestral language for the peoples of the interior, and then in Greek under Titus's signature. The consensus removes the Jesus and John passages from the evidence because it reads them as Christian, reads what remains as a medieval free translation, and takes that reading as confirming the removal. Read against the Christianity of Rus', the passages give another theology and another account: John's lawful way out from mortal masters, a man who will not take the name of man, Moses the lawgiver risen, Pilate's release of a benefactor, a resurrection reported and not confessed, an oracle left open. The essay weighs the Essene chapter's nine divergences in a ledger that holds the medieval account to the same standard as the proposal. It sets the changes no medieval interest explains against what the interpolation claim has demonstrated: three reported sources, a set of asserted likenesses, and the rest assigned by subject alone. Part II reads the Slavonic hedge at the wonder-worker as a mirror of Catullus 51: in Catullus flesh becomes word, and in the Slavonic effective word acquires a human biography. Version 1.0 (#626) and version 2.0 (#1761) stay on the record.

methodology: Close reading of the Slavonic War in Meshcherskii's Old Russian, by line of the seated text, against the Greek War (Niese, seated), Berendts and Grass's German collation, Thackeray's English, Hippolytus's Refutatio, the Dead Sea Scrolls, Philo, Eusebius, Epiphanius and George the Monk. Every quotation of a primary text was checked against a seated text or a printed page. The Acta Pilati Greek was checked on Tischendorf 1876, p. 314, and George the Monk on de Boor 1904, pp. 328–331. The Essene argument is stated as inference to the best explanation, divergence by divergence, with the best medieval alternative and a defeat condition for each. The scope of the changes is tested against the predictions of two accounts.
falsification_conditions: Section II states, for each Essene divergence, what would decide it either way. The medieval account is held to the same standard as the proposal, and an alternative that is only available is recorded as available. The collation of the Slavonic against Refutatio IX 18–28 whole is investigated, not decided: matter peculiar to Hippolytus found in the Slavonic would support contact. An item of the Jesus and John passages leaves the evidence when a medieval source for it is shown and the direction of borrowing established. Pichkhadze's three reported sources are the first to be read. Part II is doctrinal reconstruction and claims no route of transmission.

wiki_article: The Word That Became Text is a two-part essay by Johannes Sigil and Rebekah Cranes, designated EA-LOGOS-01. Version 2.1 was deposited on 12 November 2026. It succeeds version 2.0 (#1761) and version 1.0 (#626), which stay on the record. Part I contests the consensus that the divergences of the Slavonic Jewish War from the Greek are a medieval translator's work. It reads the Old Russian from N. A. Meshcherskii's edition, seated as EA-CORPORA-37 (#1760). It starts from Josephus's own testimony that he wrote the War twice, first in his ancestral language for the peoples of the interior and then in Greek under Titus's signature. It shows the consensus to be circular: the Jesus and John passages are removed from the evidence because they are read as Christian, and the remainder is read as a medieval free translation that confirms the removal. Read against the Christianity of Rus', the passages give another theology and another account. John offers a lawful way out from mortal masters and calls himself a man. The wonder-worker cannot be called a man, and his followers call him Moses risen. Pilate releases him as a benefactor, the resurrection is reported and not confessed, and the oracle is left open. The essay weighs the Essene chapter's divergences in a ledger that holds the medieval account to the same standard as the proposal. The night office has a parallel in George the Monk's chronicle, available and not shown to be used; the agreements with Hippolytus have none. It sets the changes no medieval interest explains, among them the martyrs of 4 Maccabees in that book's words and the count at Jotapata, against what the interpolation claim has demonstrated: three reported sources, a set of asserted likenesses, and the rest assigned by subject. Part II, in a doctrinal register, reads the Slavonic hedge 'if it is fitting to call him a man' as a mirror of Catullus 51: in Catullus flesh becomes word, and in the Slavonic effective word acquires a human biography.

errata.was: the break from the consensus re-derived as a testable proposal; the wonder-worker read as a man whose works outrun the name, with the Word as the reading's gloss; Sappho 31 set as a triangle of lover, beloved and rival; the doctrine's lineage without Philo
errata.now: Version 2.2 (#1764) reads from the standing of the Historical Logos (#1757), Revelation First (#1755) and the Tenth Muse (#1756). The wonder-worker is Philo's Logos, named and refused in Philo's terms and written as a man at the hedge. The veil is the cosmos the Logos wears, torn, and the temple behind it is the Apocalypse's. The seats of fragment 31 are the Tenth Muse's; the lineage follows the Historical Logos's stations.
errata.reason: At the author's word, 2026-11-12: 'we need to ground in the existing framework, and make sure we are not reinventing the break from consensus with every fresh reading.'
